metadata.title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Ramp Metering Based on Traffic Video Data

hyperparameters.name: N (consecutive time steps for state)
hyperparameters.context: State representation for the DRL method, where matrices of consecutive time steps are stacked to form the state.
hyperparameters.source_quote: Since one matrix is insufficient to describe vehicle dynamics, we stack the matrices of consecutive N time steps to represent the state st: St = {mt-(N-1),..., mt}.

hyperparameters.name: Uv (constant for vehicle representation)
hyperparameters.context: Used in the position matrix to represent vehicles in the control area.
hyperparameters.source_quote: mt(x, y) = Uv, i E It, where Uv is a constant

metadata.hardware_requirements: The training process, presented in Figure 8, can be finished in less than 24 hours on a computing server with NVIDIA Quadro K620 GPU and Intel Xeon CPU E5-1650 (3.6 GHz, 6 cores).

nodes_source.source_quote: In this work, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method to explore the potential of traffic video data in improving the efficiency of ramp metering.
nodes_source.description: Real-world traffic video data from which vehicle locations are extracted and reformed as position matrices, used as inputs for the deep reinforcement learning method.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: The data used to support the results of this study are available from the corresponding author upon request.

nodes_process.node_name: Extract vehicle locations and form state matrices
nodes_process.source_quote: Vehicle locations are extracted from the traffic video frames and are reformed as position matrices.
nodes_process.description: Vehicle locations are extracted from raw traffic video frames. These locations are used to create position matrices, which represent the traffic state at a given time step. Consecutive matrices are stacked, and down-sampling is applied to reduce input dimensions.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, no tools named, 0/4 params stated (X, Y, N implied but no values, down-sampling factor missing).

nodes_process.source_quote: the Q-network in Mnih et al. [30] is revised as Figure 7, which consists of three convolutional neural network (CNN) layers and one full connection (FC) layer for each output layer.
nodes_process.description: The Q-network architecture is a revised version of the one from Mnih et al. [30]. It comprises three convolutional neural network (CNN) layers and one fully connected (FC) layer for each output layer. The CNN layers extract features, and the FC layers estimate Q-values, speed, and queue length.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, all tools implied, all params stated from Figure 7.

nodes_process.node_name: Train Deep Q-learning model for ramp metering
nodes_process.source_quote: The algorithm for training the ramp metering policy is presented in Algorithm 1.
nodes_process.description: The Deep Q-learning model is trained using a gradient-based algorithm (Adam) to minimize a loss function. It incorporates experience replay and a target network for stability, and a multitask learning strategy to simultaneously predict Q-values, mean speed, and queue length.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, 1/5 tools named, 10/12 params stated (num_training_episodes, num_decision_time_steps_per_episode missing).

nodes_process.source_quote: The PI-ALINEA method fixes the length of the green phase and determines the length of the red phase in the current signal cycle based on the length of the red phase in the previous cycle and the downstream occupancies in the previous and current cycles.
nodes_process.description: The PI-ALINEA method is a rule-based ramp metering algorithm. It fixes the green phase length and calculates the red phase length for the current cycle based on the previous red phase length and downstream occupancies. It uses regulator parameters to minimize mean travel times.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, no tools named, all params stated.

nodes_process.node_name: Set up SUMO traffic simulation environment
nodes_process.source_quote: The proposed method is evaluated in SUMO, an open-source microscopic traffic simulator [31].
nodes_process.description: A microscopic traffic simulator (SUMO) is used to create the road network, including a one-lane on-ramp and a three-lane mainline merging into a three-lane freeway. Driving behaviors are calibrated based on empirical data.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, 1/1 tool named, 4/5 params stated (driving behavior parameters missing).

nodes_process.source_quote: The Q-network is trained in 106 training frames, and each scenario is evaluated in 20 simulation experiments.
nodes_process.description: The trained DRL model is evaluated within the SUMO simulation environment. The evaluation involves running 20 simulation experiments, each initialized with different random seeds, to assess the model's performance.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, 1/2 tools named, 1/2 params stated (random_seed not specified).

nodes_process.source_quote: the second scenario adopts the PI-ALINEA method.
nodes_process.description: The PI-ALINEA model is evaluated within the SUMO simulation environment. This involves running 20 simulation experiments, each initialized with different random seeds, to assess its performance as a comparative baseline.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, 1/2 tools named, 1/2 params stated (random_seed not specified).

nodes_process.source_quote: The first scenario does not apply ramp metering
nodes_process.description: A no-control scenario, where no ramp metering is applied, is evaluated within the SUMO simulation environment. This serves as a baseline for comparison, running 20 simulation experiments with different random seeds.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, 1/2 tools named, 1/2 params stated (random_seed not specified).

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 9 presents the Q1 (25%), Q2 (50%), and Q3 (75%) of the travel times in the mainline for three scenarios.
nodes_process.description: Mainline travel times from the DRL method, PI-ALINEA method, and no-control scenario are compared. The Q1, Q2 (median), and Q3 percentiles of travel times are presented to show performance and stability.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, no tools named, no params required.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 10 presents the temporal-spatial distribution of the mean speeds along the mainline.
nodes_process.description: The temporal-spatial distribution of mean speeds along the mainline is compared across the DRL method, PI-ALINEA method, and no-control scenario to demonstrate efficiency and performance.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, no tools named, no params required.

nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 11 presents the Q1, Q2, and Q3 of the queue lengths at the on-ramp in three scenarios.
nodes_process.description: The Q1, Q2 (median), and Q3 percentiles of queue lengths at the on-ramp are compared for the DRL method, PI-ALINEA method, and no-control scenario to assess vehicle delays.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, no tools named, no params required.

nodes_process.node_name: Compare queue length and red ratio relationship
nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 12 presents the mean queue lengths at the on-ramp and the red ratios (i.e., the proportion of the red phase in the simulation time) in each simulation for the two ramp metering methods.
nodes_process.description: The relationship between mean queue lengths at the on-ramp and the red ratios (proportion of red phase in simulation time) is compared for the DRL and PI-ALINEA ramp metering methods.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, no tools named, no params required.

nodes_process.node_name: Compare queue length and occupancy relationship
nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 13 presents the queue lengths at the on-ramp and the occupancy downstream of the merging area for the two ramp metering methods.
nodes_process.description: The relationship between queue lengths at the on-ramp and the occupancy downstream of the merging area is compared for the DRL and PI-ALINEA ramp metering methods.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, no tools named, no params required.

nodes_process.source_quote: The better performance of the proposed DRL method is further revealed when considering traffic flows downstream of the merge area, which is demonstrated in Figure 14.
nodes_process.description: Traffic flows downstream of the merge area are compared for the DRL method, PI-ALINEA method, and no-control scenario to demonstrate the DRL method's ability to alleviate capacity drop.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, no tools named, no params required.

nodes_process.source_quote: A perturbation analysis is conducted to evaluate the impact of information contained in video data. As shown in Figure 15, the control area is divided into eight subareas.
nodes_process.description: The control area is divided into eight subareas. Perturbed data is generated by removing information from specific subareas of the original traffic video data to evaluate the impact of different information sources.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, no tools named, 1/1 param stated.

nodes_process.node_name: Evaluate DRL model with perturbed data
nodes_process.source_quote: missing information for each subarea is evaluated in 20 simulation experiments with perturbed data.
nodes_process.description: The trained DRL model is evaluated using the perturbed traffic video data within the SUMO simulation environment. This involves 20 simulation experiments for each subarea's perturbation.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, 1/2 tools named, 1/2 params stated (random_seed not specified).

nodes_process.node_name: Compare travel times from perturbation analysis
nodes_process.source_quote: Figure 16 presents the box plot of travel time when the information of different subareas is removed, and the baseline is the result of experiments that take original data as input.
nodes_process.description: Travel times from the DRL model evaluated with perturbed data (information removed from different subareas) are compared against a baseline using original data. Results are presented as a box plot.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, no tools named, no params required.
